paragraphs: As to what he has claimed — that what drove our co-religionists to take up the doctrine of qiyās was that they were ducking the consequence of acknowledging the Mishnah and Talmud — that is an assertion without proof. Our co-religionists rejected the Mishnah and Talmud for two reasons. First: these are not books of revelation; the prophets did not bring them. They are books composed, attributed to a school of men; and we will demonstrate the unsoundness of the claim that they are transmitted from the prophets (in the place where that is to be done).[{2}] Second: they contain manifestly false and impossible statements, some of which we have already mentioned and others of which we will mention in the coming chapters. So once our co-religionists saw this, and saw that the argument from analogy (which is the argument from al-ʿaql) is binding and admits no impeachment from reason — that it is the standing measure of every assertion — they took hold of qiyās and abandoned what is plainly false. They retained only what could not be impeached by reason; and indeed the very ground of his complaint binds him, not us. For the ancients to whom he ascribes his teachings, those whom he claims to be the aṣḥāb al-āthār wa-l-nāqila (the people of oral-tradition transmission), did not themselves disavow qiyās: it is everywhere in their statements and writings, and their school's positions are built on it. We will mention a portion of that in due course. So one who rejects qiyās — and claims that this is the doctrine of the ancients — has contradicted himself. As for what he reports about Anan and the "two tablets": Anan did not in fact argue from this for the establishment of qiyās; so we have no need to mention what [Saadia] says about it.[{3}]

As for his claim that taftīsh (searching) cannot refer to the bringing-forth of something non-existent: the matter is not as he says. Scripture itself: "And they search out devices, perfecting the diligent search" (Ps 64:7) — here it reports that they search after things that have arisen in their imagination, things that arise in the heart; and this parallels Ezek 20:32, "and that which arises in your spirit," and continues "we have completed the searching of the searcher." That is not a self-subsistent thing being searched for. Similarly: "the lamp of the Lord is the soul of man, searching all the inward parts of the belly" (Prov 20:27); and "Let us search and try our ways" (Lam 3:40). If someone replies that all these are existent things [that exist as inner states or paths], we reply: very well — but the realities of the commandments and the prohibitions are likewise subsistent in themselves; they are simply hidden from most people, until those people search and investigate, and so bring them forth and disclose them. The Sage himself attests to this: after he said (Prov 2:4), "Search her as hidden treasure," he said immediately: "then shalt thou understand the fear of the Lord."[{4}] He thus reports that if you seek wisdom and the knowledge of the commandments, and search for them, you will then understand the knowledge of God and the fear of Him. A clearer instance still: David says, "And I commune with my own heart, and my spirit searches" (Ps 77:7). What is he searching after? He explains: "Will the Lord cast off forever?" (Ps 77:8) — this is not an existent thing, but a contemplative question: is this so, or not? So taftīsh in Scripture can perfectly well designate the search for the as-yet-unknown — and this is what qiyās does.

As for what he said about Deut 22:26 — "did the Eternal do this analogy because it was obligatory upon Him, or because it was not?" — that is itself an unsound question, a bad form of words. It is impermissible to ask of God: "did He do what was obligatory upon Him to do, or not?" If that kind of question were permitted in the case of qiyās, the same form of question would be permitted in every commandment and prohibition. Did the command to Abraham to circumcise on the eighth day arise because it was obligatory upon God? Then why did He not command it before the birth of Ishmael — so that Ishmael, too, could have been circumcised on the eighth day? Or did He do it because it was not obligatory upon Him? Then the eight-day circumcision-command is non-obligatory, and that does not concede anything against us. The same form of question can be raised about every divine command. Indeed: did God do for man at maturity what He did — granting him ʿaql and the obligation of the law — because it was obligatory, or because it was not? If obligatory, why not earlier? If not, then making man rational is non-obligatory, etc. Of this kind of self-defeating question there is an endless supply. God (mighty and exalted) commands what He wills and does what He wills of wisdom, rightness, and justice — without the question of "obligatory or not obligatory upon Him" being raised.[{5}]

As to his saying that "if it was obligatory upon Him, He cannot initiate a precept except by qiyās on a prior" — that is a false analogy. The opponent has the option to say: it is obligatory upon Him in the second case (the case to which one is reasoning) but not in the first (the case from which one is reasoning). For qiyās is the building of a structure on a foundation: where there is no foundation, no building can rise on it. Qiyās takes effect on an uṣūl on which it is reasoned. Where there is no uṣūl yet posited, there is nothing to reason from. So Saadia's counter — which depends on the symmetry of the two cases — is itself unsound.

As for what he counter-argued from the alleged refutation of the origination of things: it operates against him, not against us. For God (mighty and exalted) created the uṣūl — that is, the four elements and natures — ex nihilo, and then created the rest of things from their composition and admixture. Just so: He commanded farāʾiḍ ex nihilo, without their being analogically grounded on anything else, and made them into foundations from which the further matters are taken by qiyās on what He has posited. We can then counter him with his own move: tell us about God's creation of plants and animals out of the elements — did He do this because it was obligatory upon Him, or because it was not obligatory? If obligatory, He cannot initiate a creation without a prior foundation — and that yields the eternity of created things alongside the Creator. If not obligatory, then He has done it non-obligatorily; and likewise He has done qiyās non-obligatorily, no difference.

As to his statement, "tell us what agreement (wifāq) there is between murder and fornication" — that is the statement of a man who has not understood the form of qiyās under discussion (or who is being deliberately tendentious). The Karaites never claimed that the qiyās was between murder as such and fornication as such. The wifāq is between one coerced person and another coerced person: between coercion and coercion, seizure (ghaṣb) and seizure. The argument is this: if a man falls upon someone and the assaulted one has no power to fend him off and so is killed, the murdered man is excused; he is not held to a culpable surrender of his own life, since he was coerced (maghṣūb ʿalā nafsihi) — he had no power to fend off the attack. Were he able to fend it off and did not, then he would have been culpable for handing over his life; but since he could not, he is excused. So Scripture says: "thus is the case of this betrothed maiden seized by force; since she had no power to fend off her assailant, and there was no one to come to her aid, she is excused — not pursued." This is the qiyās by application of cause to effect; and this kind of qiyās admits no impeachment. It is the strongest of all the forms of qiyās, and it is plain. What Saadia has said about it is null and contributes nothing to the discussion.

As to his saying that "like one who rises against his neighbor" is not categorical (ḥatm) but probabilistic (imkān) — we say in reply: the Torah's ruling on this maiden, and its distinction between her case in the field and her case in the city, is in fact stated on the generality of normal occurrence. It is possible that the matter went otherwise. So if upon investigation it became clear that the maiden in the city had been forcibly violated and prevented from crying out (or had cried out and no one heard her), then she is not to be condemned; and if upon investigation it became clear that the maiden in the field had consented, she would not be acquitted. This itself — the procedure of investigation upon a presumptive ruling — is the strongest indication of the obligation of qiyās.

As to his saying, "even if Scripture itself made qiyās, we cannot make qiyās, just as Scripture initiated the law and we cannot initiate" — we say: where is this premise from, and how was it derived? Qiyās is not initiation. Initiation, as we are informed, is the positing of a foundation, a basis on which things are built. Qiyās is built on something else, on a foundation already posited. So the Creator may initiate legislation, and we may then learn to analogize on the foundation He has set, just as He Himself analogized on what He had earlier set. Moreover: if his argument were sound, it would also follow that, since the Creator commands and forbids, we may not command and forbid; but in fact every legal scholar commands and forbids on the strength of what the Creator commanded and forbade. So Saadia's argument, if pressed, eliminates the very practice of fiqh that Saadia himself engages in.

As to his saying, "how is qiyās in the laws permissible when the laws are not themselves set on analogy?" — we have already explained that this is incoherent. For if the laws were set on analogy, they would not be uṣūl — they would themselves be furūʿ built on prior uṣūl. Since they are the uṣūl, and qiyās is built upon them, it is not requisite that they be set on analogy. To require otherwise is to require an infinite regress. This is exactly parallel to rational knowledge. Our rational knowledge is built on sensory knowledge, which is ḍarūrī and immediate, not analogical. If Saadia's argument applied, rational knowledge itself would be impossible — for rational knowledge is not built on yet-other-rational knowledge but on non-rational ḍarūrī sense-knowledge, which is not itself derivative. So just as rational analogical knowledge in the natural sciences is built on the non-analogical ḍarūrī given by sense, analogical halakhic knowledge is built on the non-analogical naṣṣ given by revelation. The structure is exactly the same.

As to what he said about the three forms of qiyās and the four causes — "if we apply the four causes to the laws, we find the laws contradict them" — and his example of the cloven-hoofed cud-chewer (which can still be carrion, torn, or sanctified, and thus forbidden): praise be to God, what an astonishing argument from a man of his calibre! Does he not know that our Book — and the farāʾiḍ and prohibitions in it — qualify one another; that no precept is fully known until one has followed everything the Book says about it in all the places it says anything? If that is so, then the cause of permission to eat is not simply "cloven-hoofed and cud-chewing." It is that, plus "not carrion," plus "not torn," plus "not sanctified," plus "properly slaughtered," plus other conditions still — "not slaughtered before the eighth day from birth" (Lev 22:27), "not slaughtered while pregnant," and so on. The combination of all these together is the cause of permission; the meat is permitted only when all these conditions are jointly satisfied — not when only some are. In this lies the rebuttal of everything he said about the formal cause too. Scripture's report (Lev 13:13) that the leper is pure when whiteness covers his entire body shows that the cause of impurity is not "whiteness simpliciter" but "whiteness combined with sound flesh." Likewise his point about the priest and the meal-offering: the cause of the priest's eating is not simply that he offers the meal-offering, but that he offers it for someone else; if it is his own, the cause that licenses eating is dissolved. Likewise the final cause: the altar's purpose is to receive the peace-offering — but the cause's operativeness is on the day that admits the offering; if it is the Sabbath, on which peace-offerings cannot be offered, the operative cause has been removed.

It is as if he sensed what is binding upon him from what we have just said, for he then conceded: "if anyone supposes he can escape by saying these conditions are merely restrictions of the causes, like exceptions — we reply, in that very fact they cease to be causes-and-principles in the report-based precept." But this is mere relabeling. The fact that we describe the conditions as part of the cause rather than exceptions to it does not change the analysis. Whatever we call the proviso, the structural fact is the same: a precept can have more than one operative cause-condition, and the joint satisfaction of all of them constitutes the actual ground of the ruling. Saadia himself, in his counter-argument from "cloven-hoofed and cud-chewing," cites two conditions that jointly obligate the permission. If two conditions are admitted, more than two are admitted a fortiori. There is no way out for him.

As to his point about jadalī qiyās (the application of cause to effect) — and his rebuttal from Gen 9:6, that the protection of human blood has as its cause man's being "in the noble image," yet the disbeliever's and the murderer's blood may be shed — we reply within the same framework: the cause of the prohibition of murder is not "being in the noble image" alone. It is "being in the noble image and being innocent" — for Scripture says (Exod 23:7): "And the innocent and the righteous slay thou not." When transgression is committed, one of the two causes that jointly required protection has fallen. Furthermore, Saadia has erred twice over here. First, he has classed murder among the samʿī (revealed-only) precepts, but on the standard taxonomy murder is ʿaqlī — even the strongest version of his position would concede this. Second, he has misread the cause-clause of Gen 9:6: the cause is not "image therefore preserve" but "image therefore retribution-is-to-be-exacted" — for the verse reads: "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the noble image He made man." The "image" clause grounds the obligation of retributive justice, not the absolute inviolability of the blood.

The same reply applies to his case of the slave who dies after two days (Exod 21:21, "for he is his money"). The text attaches this to its companion clause: "if he remains a day or two." Two causes: (i) the slave's surviving a day or two, and (ii) being the master's property. If the slave is the master's property but does not survive a day or two, one of the two operative conditions for non-retribution is dissolved.

As to the prohibition of the granddaughter (Lev 18:10) as "your nakedness," together with the licit status of the wife despite the same designation "your nakedness" (Lev 18:8) — though the term is the same, the underlying cause is different. The granddaughter is "the grandfather's nakedness" because she has proceeded from his loins — and the cause of her being his "nakedness" is consanguinity through descent. The same applies to the grandmother: her grandson is her "nakedness" by the same cause of descent.[{6}] But the wife is "the husband's nakedness" by an entirely different cause: she has become one flesh with him (Gen 2:24, "and they shall be one flesh"). The cause of this unity-of-flesh relation is the conjugal union, not consanguinity. The two relations — though both called "your nakedness" in Hebrew — operate on different causes; what is prohibited in the one case (consanguinity through descent) is what is permitted in the other (conjugal union). There is no contradiction in the cause-structure once we identify the actual cause-clauses correctly. The same line of reading resolves all the cases Saadia adduced. If we replied to all of them as we replied above (§10) — that the cause is compound, not single — that alone would suffice; but the present reading shows that even where the language of the cause-clause is the same, the cause itself can differ.

As to the prohibition of the maternal and paternal aunts ("your kinswoman," Lev 18:12–13, and Lev 20:19–20 "for he hath uncovered his kin's nakedness"), and the licit status of the daughter of one's uncle (which Saadia claims is implied by Lev 25:49, "or any near of his kin") — by my life,[{7}] this is a sophistry that catches many people, but the reply is decisive: Scripture's phrase "or any near of his kin" does not refer to the relative himself; it refers to the relative-of-the-relative-just-named. The verse-context (Lev 25:48–49) is the order of redeemers: "his brother shall redeem him, or his uncle, or his cousin, or any near of his kin." Scripture started with the brother — closest — then uncle, then cousin. The phrase "or any near of his kin" picks up after the cousin, and refers to those next in the descending series of kinship.[{8}] The same parsing-logic resolves Lev 15:9–10: "And every saddle on which the issuing-one rides shall be unclean," then (v. 10) "and whoever touches anything that is under him" — where "him" does not refer to the issuing-one, but to the saddle just named. Misreading the antecedent has produced Saadia's objection. These two examples — the aunts/cousins and the saddle — are the strongest of the cases Saadia adduces; once they are answered, the rest of his case collapses.

As to what he said about the three forms of qiyās and the long list of test-cases — distinguishing two equals, equating two distincts, and so on — our reply to all of them is the same: these are all exceptions (istithnāʾ) to the qiyās that Saadia adduced. This may sound strange. Many who hear it for the first time recoil from it; only on reflection does the sense become clear. So we offer the following ground for it: scriptural qiyās — as we have explained above — is built upon the naṣṣ; the naṣṣ itself is its foundation; and naṣṣ itself admits of exceptions. Since naṣṣ admits exceptions, qiyās — which is a branch built upon naṣṣ — admits exceptions a fortiori. Example: Scripture says of the Sabbath (Exod 20:10), "Thou shalt do no manner of work." The plain meaning would forbid every act of work. But Scripture itself makes an exception by allowing the offering of sacrifices on the Sabbath — which combines many works (Num 28:10, "the burnt-offering of every Sabbath in his Sabbath"). So naṣṣ itself exhibits the same kind of exception-pattern Saadia attributes to qiyās: it can be obligatory that the thief of the ox restore five, and qiyās would obligate the same in the case of the ram; but Scripture has excepted the ram and made the penalty four. The garment-thief and the donkey-thief are equally bound by the same two-fold restitution, though qiyās would distinguish them. And so on through all of Saadia's cases.[{9}] If we limited ourselves to this single reply for all his cases, it would suffice and would dispatch everything he supposed binds us.

We have already alerted you that this bab is subtle; those who comment on it and those who follow this argument must apprehend it well. They should — when commenting — bring forward the texts with their exceptions together, and then carry over the farāʾiḍ that qiyās obligates onto that frame. If one does this, and exposits the matter well, no opponent will be able to dislodge him.

As to his point about reasoning a fortiori — the wife whose husband charges her with being unfaithful (the moṣiʾ shem raʿ of Deut 22:13–19, penalty 100 silver) vs. the adulterer in the father's house (Deut 22:28–29, penalty 50 silver) — and his claim that qiyās would obligate a worse penalty on the actor than on the suspecter: The reply is that the husband's claim against his wife is the claim of a party to the dispute (khaṣm), not the testimony of witnesses; rulings are not effected on the basis of one party's claim but on the basis of evidence. If a man claims that another has stolen a hundred dinars from him and the claim turns out to be false, the false claimant has no penalty imposed on him. If a witness testifies that he stole, and the testimony is shown to be false-perjury, the witness is bound to pay the hundred dinars (cf. Deut 19:18–19), but the original claimant is not. The husband's case is that of a claimant — not a witness — and is therefore on a different footing.

As to the leprosy case, we have already addressed it. As to the case of janābah and excrement — the obligation to wash after seminal emission but not after defecation — this does not obligate qiyās either way: the cause for washing after janābah may be other than what he mentioned (the emission of fluid from the body's substance, whereas excrement is foreign-food residue). Even on his reading, this is at worst an exception of the kind we have allowed. As to Ammon and Moab vs. Edom (Deut 23:4–9): the offense of Ammon and Moab was not merely the intent to harm but the active withholding of food and water — leading to death (Deut 23:5, "because they met you not with bread and with water in the way"). Edom, by contrast, merely prevented passage (Num 20:18–21); they did not actively try to starve Israel. So the asymmetric treatment of the two has a sufficient cause; the qiyās is not violated.

As to the water-of-purification (Num 19): that it purifies the impure and renders impure the pure (the bearer-of-the-ash) — this is one of the secrets (asrār) of Scripture, whose true rationale none knows except God and those of His prophets and saints to whom He has disclosed it. To attack qiyās on the basis of this case is, in effect, to attack the whole of religion — for the red-heifer-water case is precisely one that resists both naṣṣ-interpretation and qiyās-interpretation alike. So Saadia's objection here is misplaced.

We add this: even if Saadia had made his case for the "weighty and light" objection — which is a fortiori reasoning — that would itself impeach him, for qal va-ḥomer is precisely one of the standard hermeneutical canons of his own Rabbanite tradition. In the opening of Sifra — the baraita of R. Ishmael, which the Rabbanites cite at the very head of Torat Kohanim — it is written: "of the thirteen canons by which the Torah is interpreted: the qiyās al-manṭiqī [i.e., qal va-ḥomer]…". The Rabbanite tradition opens its hermeneutic with logical analogy! Saadia's argument therefore impeaches his own school as much as it impeaches us.[{10}] He has not noticed this, or has hoped his readers would not notice.
The differential treatment of men and women in the law (Saadia's §15) — same answer: these are exceptions, istithnāʾāt, and we have already explained the principle.

Returning to what he claimed about the rational commandments: some scholars deny that there is any purely rational commandment except the knowledge of the Creator, the doctrine of His unity, what may and may not be ascribed to Him, and the reprehensibility of lying.[{11}] As for what some hold to be ʿaqlī — the prohibition of murder, fornication, and theft — we ourselves never knew the reprehensibility of these by way of reason; we knew them only by way of revelation, which is the divine command. Those who hold them to be ʿaqlī argue: "we observe that whoever claims their prohibition by reason, when asked for proof, replies: we do not love that we ourselves be killed, nor that one we love be killed; we do not love that anyone violate someone we love, nor that one steal our money; we hold whoever does this to us to be a wrongdoer; injustice is reprehensible to our reason; therefore we ourselves should not do these things to others, since to do so is itself injustice." But the argument as stated also implies the opposite. If everything that brings pleasure is correspondingly required by reason — since we are entitled to seek what removes our suffering — then it would be required by reason to steal in order to remove the pain of hunger, to kill the enemy in order to obtain security, and so forth. That would be a contradiction of the original premise.

Furthermore: if murder and the appropriation of property were reprehensible by reason and forbidden by reason, then it would not be possible for Scripture to render them licit or to abrogate them in some respect — just as lying, mocking the Creator, and ingratitude for His bounty cannot be rendered licit on any account, being intrinsically reprehensible in reason. Yet Scripture in fact does license killing — namely the killing of the children of the seven Canaanite nations (Deut 20:16–17), who committed no transgression of their own.[{12}] If revelation can license the killing of innocent children, then murder is not reprehensible by reason categorically. And if murder is not categorically ʿaqlī, a fortiori neither are fornication and theft. So the question for Saadia is this: given his own two-categories doctrine, which he has not securely founded, by what principle does he hold that qiyās applies to the ʿaqlī commandments but not to the samʿī ones? Who licensed him to draw the line at exactly that place? On his own argument, both kinds of commandment are obligated by the same God; if qiyās is licit in the one, why not in the other? We now turn — having dispatched Saadia's argument — to some of the precepts that themselves necessitate qiyās, and to what the Rabbanites of an earlier era said that obligates it.
